title: Abigail Adams: "Remember the Ladies"
text:
John and Abigail Adams married in 1764 and spent much of their marriage apart. While John served in the Continental Congress in Philadelphia, Abigail ran the family farm at Braintree, Massachusetts, raised four children, dealt with tenants, debts and war shortages, and wrote him letters full of news, politics and argument. More than a thousand of their letters survive.

On 31 March 1776, as Congress moved toward independence, Abigail wrote to John: "in the new Code of Laws which I suppose it will be necessary for you to make I desire you would Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors." She warned him not to put unlimited power into the hands of husbands, since "all Men would be tyrants if they could," and joked that the ladies would foment a rebellion of their own if they were ignored.

John replied on 14 April that he could only laugh at her "extraordinary Code of Laws," though he added that men knew better than to repeal their masculine systems, which in practice left them only the name of masters. Abigail did not let it go. She complained to her friend Mercy Otis Warren about his answer.

The marriage remained a partnership of two strong minds. John called her his "dearest friend" and relied on her judgment all his life, through his presidency and beyond. Her letter is still quoted as one of the earliest American appeals for women's rights.
lesson: The best partners challenge each other honestly, even on things they will not win at once. A marriage of minds is one in which both voices are heard.
source: Adams Family Correspondence, vol. 1 (Massachusetts Historical Society); Abigail Adams to John Adams, 31 March 1776
